name: The governor (ʿāmil)
definition: What brings about the iʿrāb of a word: the word (or the meaning) that puts it in rafʿ, naṣb, jarr or jazm.
body: Iʿrāb, in the madrasa's definition, is the change of a word's ending because of the governors that come upon it. The governor is the cause; the word it governs is the maʿmūl; the ending it brings is the ʿamal, the work. In قَامَ زَيْدٌ the verb قَامَ governs زَيْدٌ and gives it rafʿ.

Most governors are words you can see (lafẓī): verbs, the particles of jarr, inna and its sisters, the particles that put the muḍāriʿ in naṣb or jazm. A few are meanings (maʿnawī): the mubtadaʾ is in rafʿ because it stands at the head free of any governor (al-ibtidāʾ), and the muḍāriʿ is in rafʿ when nothing puts it in naṣb or jazm.

The idea is old, but two books made it a course of its own: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī's al-ʿAwāmil al-miʾa, a hundred governors, read in the Indian madrasa, and Imām Birgivī's al-ʿAwāmil al-jadīda, sixty governors with the governed and the states of iʿrāb, the first book of naḥw of the Ottoman madrasa.

examples.text: Zayd stood: the verb is the governor, zaydun the governed, in rafʿ.
I passed by Zayd: the particle bi- governs zaydin and puts it in jarr.
